x: Inefficiencies in various parts of the shipping world continues to keep freight on a tight leash.  The strength is coming from a strong arb, tight shipping availability driven by Panama Canal restrictions and subsequently with both ballast and laden legs increasingly routed via Cape. TS Edouard's impact is reportedly limited to the Sabine Pass.  With August loadings complete, routing shows roughly 30 of 110 departures via Cape to discharge East, against Panama Canal auction fee levels and transit uncertainty.  Whilst there are only a couple September vessels left, fixing activity pivots to October. The October position list now shows 2 first-decade, 7 second-decade, 1 third-decade. In other words, very tight availability for spot shipping.
Strong

The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the gains broadening across both basins as the index pushed higher over successive sessions. In the Atlantic the tone is constructive: transatlantic business remains well bid on the back of a replenished cargo book and a tightening nearby tonnage list, while fronthaul has been slower to follow, with owners holding above charterers' ideas on US Gulf and South American grain. The Pacific has been the stronger of the two, where a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal alongside North Pacific grain has left prompt tonnage short and charterers chasing owners' levels rather than the reverse. Period interest has picked up markedly, with a good spread of owners collecting for both short and twelve-month cover and bids increasingly obliged to follow last-done rather than set it, although the forward curve continues to price modest backwardation beyond the prompt. We expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the main question being how much of the recent move reflects genuine incremental demand rather than positioning ahead of the autumn grain programme.

The Supramax market remained mixed and largely directionless, with activity picking up selectively across both the Atlantic and Asia. The Atlantic saw pockets of strength, particularly around the USG and South Atlantic, supported by steady demand for grains, petcoke and minor bulks, while Asia remained active but positional with varied tonnage availability between areas. Handysize trading was generally subdued, although fundamentals remained healthy in parts of the Pacific and South Atlantic. The US Gulf continued to show relatively firm conditions despite limited fixing, while the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained softer. Overall, sentiment across both sectors remains cautious, with regional tonnage positioning and pockets of enquiry driving the market rather than any clear broader trend. There is good appetite for period with quite a few fixtures reported past weeks.

Capesize is heating up across all segments, with both C3 and C5 trade routes posting some of the highest numbers seen this year. Last done on C3 Brazil/China today was seen at USD 40.9, setting a new benchmark which hasn't been seen since the peak of 2021. FFAs are up for the coming quarter, Baltic C3 prints USD 40.2 today and C5 is also showing strong activity with last done in the mid USD 16s and rumors of a fixture at USD 17 flat (yet to be confirmed). C5 West Australia/China prints USD 16.5 today on the Baltic, jumping 7.59% today, overtaking C3 Brazil/China as the higher earner per day between C3 and C5. With an uptick of ballasters headed for Brazil toward the end of September, we may see some pressure in the Atlantic for late September and early October laycans. Overall sentiment is bullish but cautious as limited fresh demand to absorb growing supply.

The September list is down to 10 vessels, and October dates are starting to come into view. Panama NB/SB fees remain a real dissuader, and it's showing up in the routing split: ballasters from Asia are now going 50/50 Cape versus Panama, up from roughly 25% back in June and July. Fixture activity has been quiet this week, just a handful done, with owners' ideas mid/low USD 260's.

The Supramax market remained largely subdued and stable. The Atlantic was mixed, with the Mediterranean gradually softening while the Continent saw some fresh enquiry and the US Gulf and South Atlantic remained broadly balanced. In the Pacific, activity was stronger in the NOPAC and parts of Southeast Asia, while Indonesian coal activity was relatively limited. The Handysize market showed a modestly firmer tone, supported by improving cargos in East Coast South America, tighter prompt tonnage in parts of the Pacific and better sentiment in the US Gulf. While the US Gulf was still soft in the short term despite expectations of improvement ahead.

This week on Capesize we saw strong demand from Pacific C5 as three majors were seen in the market alongside a healthy showing of supportive operators. Recent bids seen at mid to high USD 15 levels and today a Newcastlemax fixed at low USD 15 C5 equivalent. Ballasters are looking to get ahead of yet another Typhoon forecasted to hit the coast of southeast China (near Fujian) around late Thursday to early Friday and recent fixtures ex West Australia have been reported in high USD 14s. Atlantic C3 Brazil/China has also seen healthy activity with rumors expecting even higher levels for October. With a flurry of fixtures yesterday, C3 ex Brazil reported levels for 2h September laycans in mid/high USD 37s with one stem reported at USD 38 for late September. Offers today reported in high USD 37 and mid USD 38s for early October laycans ex Brazil. The North Atlantic shows some fronthaul and transatlantic demand ex Seven Islands for later September dates and tonnage remains healthy in the North. A recent fixture ex Seven Islands to India was reported in low USD 42 for end September.

The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the index posting consecutive gains and sentiment improving across both basins. The Pacific has been the clearer engine: NoPac and Australian grain and coal demand has absorbed the prompt tonnage that had been weighing on the market, and owners are now comfortable holding their levels while charterers chase. In the Atlantic the North has been the steadier of the two, supported by a healthy coal and minerals programme into the Continent that has kept fronthaul well bid, while the South Atlantic has traded more sideways as the market looks toward the next grain window and owners show little urgency to discount. Period enquiry has picked up noticeably, with a wider range of owners and operators willing to engage on one-year business, although bids continue to sit modestly behind owners' ideas. With paper firmer and tonnage tightening into September, we expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer in the near term.
Increasing

Fixture activity continued this week, with several concluded, all for September dates. The position list has tightened further, down to 14 ships from yesterday's 17. Positions are stacking as: 5 ships second decade September, 6 last decade September, and 3 first decade October. FOB interest is reported for first decade September, but with no ships currently sitting in that window, it may get pushed into the second decade, adding further pressure to an already thin 5-ship count there. Fixing levels have been choppy, ranging between USD 255 and 280pmt this week, (subject to vessel type and routing options) though levels have firmed back toward USD 270pmt more recently. With fresh fixtures and a tightening list, we believe freight will stay flat. Panama Canal costs remain a live factor in routing decisions: yesterday a northbound slot auction cleared at USD 4.2m, with a southbound auction at USD 851k.

Supramax market remained broadly steady, with limited movement across most regions and only modest gains in the Atlantic. The Continent and Mediterranean continue to face pressure due to ample tonnage and limited fresh cargo input, while the South Atlantic remains more balanced but somewhat positional. In Asia, sentiment is improving, supported by better activity in NoPac and Southeast Asia, although this has yet to translate into significant rate gains.  Handy market wise- another subdued session overall, with the Continent and Mediterranean remaining soft amid limited cargo volumes. The South Atlantic and USG were broadly stable, with little change in fundamentals. Asia remained the strongest area, supported by tighter prompt tonnage and steady cargo flow, although activity remained relatively limited.

Panamax sentiment has turned more cautious this week, with the index giving back part of its recent gains and both basins trading with a softer bias. The Pacific has led the correction: prompt tonnage has accumulated across the North and South while fresh NoPac grain and Australian and Indo coal enquiry has been slow to absorb it, leaving charterers in control and the market still in search of a floor. The Atlantic has held up rather better, with ECSA fronthaul remaining the firmer leg and Continent tonnage still reasonably tight, although bid/offer have widened and fixing volumes are thin as charterers wait for the north to settle. Period discussion remains active across both Kamsarmax and Panamax, but owners are resisting the softer nearby curve and bids have yet to close the gap, so relatively little is concluding. We would expect a sideways-to-softer tone into next week, with any recovery contingent on a fresh injection of grain and coal cargo in the Pacific; in the meantime the Atlantic should continue to offer owners the better alternative.

This week markets are showing slight pressure with limited fixing today on Capesize across all segments, however markets are consistent on C3 Brazil/China with the main decline seen in Pacific C5. FFAs show slight positive sentiment in the long term although above average laden to ballast ratio of vessels heading toward the Atlantic gives a slight bearish outlook in the near future. This week sentiment has had a softer tone in the Pacific and today saw a decline on paper. Earlier fixing concluded around and just below the USD 14 range for West Australia/Qingdao. Today, two miners reported fixing at USD 13.4 yesterday and latest bids are mixed and around USD 13 to USD 14 for early September laycans. In the Atlantic, levels have remained consistent however South Brazil and West Africa to China remains subdued with limited bids and offers reported today. C3 Brazil/China sees bids and offer reported in low USD 36 levels with last done in high USD 34s on C3 for West Africa and another reported in the USD 37 range on Friday for a Newcastlemax.

WEST Activity has picked up compared to last week, with several fixtures reported after a quieter run. The near-term list remains tight and heavily relet-dependent, with positions stacking up as follows: 2 ships last decade August, 1 first decade September, 6 second decade September, and 8 last decade September. Freight is sitting around USD 280pmt, underpinned by recent fixing levels. Adding to the pressure on owners weighing routing options, this week's Panama Canal northbound slot auction cleared at a record USD 4m, making the Cape an increasingly attractive routing.  EAST East of Suez, activity remained thin, with just one fixture reported, an STS Vadinar deal concluded at USD 170pmt RT/C equivalent. With so little else crossing the tape this week, it's hard to draw much of a broader trend from a single fixture.

The Panamax market has held a constructive tone through the week, with the index grinding higher after a brief pause mid-week and both basins now pointing in the same direction. The Atlantic remains led by the fronthaul, where steady South American and Black Sea grain programmes together with a thinner list of prompt North Atlantic tonnage have allowed owners to hold their ideas and to resist on shorter transatlantic business as well. In the Pacific, sentiment has improved on the back of a fuller NoPac grain order book and firmer Australian coal demand into North Asia, with Indonesian volumes providing a steady if less dynamic floor; the gap between available tonnage and cargo requirement is narrowing and charterers are having to work harder to cover. Period enquiry is genuinely active across both Kamsarmax and Panamax, with a clear preference for index-linked structures, although owners' ideas continue to sit above where charterers are prepared to bid. We expect the market to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the fronthaul retaining a healthy premium over backhaul and tonnage supply the main variable to watch.

The Supramax market began the week on a subdued note, with limited fresh activity and sentiment generally steady across most regions. The Atlantic showed signs of increased enquiry, particularly in the Mediterranean, although a widening gap between bids and offers and softer nearby positions suggested some caution. The Continent remained largely unchanged, while Asian markets were mostly flat, with backhaul activity correcting and regional demand remaining muted.  Handysize conditions were similarly quiet, with sentiment remaining cautious in both basins. Europe faced pressure from an increase in available tonnage and limited fresh cargoes, while the USG continued to struggle with weak demand and ample vessel supply. The South Atlantic showed early signs of improvement due to a more balanced cargo-to-tonnage ratio. In Asia, demand remained steady but insufficient to materially tighten the market, resulting in an overall soft but stable tone.

This week in the Capesize market we see the lowest tonnage congestion in China following Typhoon Dolphin. The typhoon hit the coast of China later last week and has since weakened, moving inland. Ballasters heading for Brazil on C3 (Brazil/China) were welcomed to a fresh injection of cargoes this week ex Brazil and West Africa. Last night fixes concluded in the USD 35-35.5 range, with owners offering USD 36.5 and traders bidding USD 35 for C3 mid-late September dates. Today rates are flat/slightly down with Baltic printing USD 35.93 and latest offers in low USD 36 range. Pacific C5 ex West Australia/China saw significant activity yesterday in the basin with three majors in the market. One fixture was done at USD 15.5 for late August dates and an East Australian stem fixed in the mid-high USD 31s for early September. Today the Pacific has also seen a slight dip on paper with Baltic down 2% today. Latest offers are in the low mid USD 14s for late August and early September. Last fixture concluded a late August Dampier stem at USD 14.25.

The USG activity remains muted with only one fixture concluded this week at USD 280 pmt H/C. Albeit the Baltic LPG3 print have started sliding downwards, owners' and traders' freight ideas to charter out, are yet to follow. We expect more activity in the USG and USEC for September as there are a mere five fixtures concluded thus far for next month. It's worth to note that the first and second decade of September only have ten vessels open for spot (five fixed as of now for September) whereas the average number of fixtures in 2026 per first and second decade every month is twenty one(!).

The Panamax market firmed steadily through the week, with momentum broadening across both basins and owners increasingly able to hold their ground. In the Atlantic, the fronthaul grain trade remained the principal driver – a healthy flow of South American and US Gulf cargoes against a tightening tonnage list kept sentiment constructive and lifted end-month levels, even against continued charterer resistance. The Pacific firmed in tandem, underpinned by tight prompt tonnage, a steadier stream of North Pacific grain alongside Australian and Indonesian coal, and some weather-related disruption that lent owners additional confidence. Period interest was active and the bid-offer gap narrowed over the week, though owners continued to price forward cover with a firm hand and a modest premium on shorter durations. With cargo replenishment healthy in both basins and the forward curve holding a shallow backwardation, we enter next week on a constructive footing.

The Capesize market began the week on a solid footing and has continued to strengthen throughout the week setting a positive trajectory. South Atlantic and West Africa continue to underpin improvements on C3 and healthy demand also pushed rates on C5 West Australia/China. In the Atlantic, the charge was led again this week on C3 Brazil/China with a flurry of fixtures in the low-mid USD 35s yesterday and today we see owners bidding in the mid USD 35s up to USD 36 for Brazil and West Africa stems for first half September laycans. In the Pacific, some ballasters are forced to delay as Typhoon Dolphin brings severe weather off the coast of China. C5 West Australia/Qingdao shows good support with four new fixtures from one miner today as the Baltic jumps by 6.9%. Refreshed offers for late August laycans are between USD 16.5-17 and one fixture was reported at low to mid USD 16s. First half September stems see offers ease to high USD 15 levels.

The Supramax and Handymax markets remained relatively stable this week. The US Gulf continued to see the highest activity, while the Continent/Mediterranean remained balanced despite limited fresh enquiry. South America softened slightly as cargo volumes eased, and Asia remained quiet with rates edging lower. Overall, the market remains steady, although fresh cargo demand will be needed for further improvement.

Freight softened this week, with two fixtures reported at USD 280 H/C and at USD 268 H/C, both end August. Activity remains quiet ahead of the Pertamina tender result, which will likely set the tone. We see only two ships end August while we start to look to September (10 first decade, 4 second decade, 4 last decade). Panama canal auction premiums held elevated, with three NB slots clearing above $3m and two SB slots at $2.6m and $1.46m. Middle East tension remains a wildcard that could change sentiment quickly.

Supramax/Ultramax market remained under pressure, extending its recent downward trend as fresh cargo enquiry stayed limited across most regions. Atlantic sentiment continued to soften, with increasing vessel availability weighing on in despite occasional stronger fixtures. Asia remains relatively quiet. Overall, the market remains cautious with little sign of a near-term improvement in the coming weeks. The Handy market was largely unchanged, with sentiment continuing to be driven by vessel positioning rather than any meaningful shift in demand. The Continent/Mediterranean remained balanced but subdued, while the Atlantic softened further as an expanding tonnage list outpaced fresh cargo volumes. Activity in the Pacific was generally quiet, with limited fixing keeping momentum subdued.

The Panamax market softened over the course of the week, with the index easing and sentiment turning more cautious across both basins amid the seasonal summer lull. The Atlantic set the softer tone – transatlantic and fronthaul enquiry stayed thin, prompt tonnage was discounted to secure employment, and a widening gap between owners' ideas and charterers' bids kept activity subdued, even as the Continent and Western Mediterranean remained comparatively tight on prompt vessels. The Pacific was the more constructive corner late in the week, steadying off recent lows as North Pacific grain enquiry improved and charterers returned to cover weather-disrupted positions, though an ample tonnage list and still-elevated Chinese stockpiles capped the recovery. Period interest remained active, with charterers continuing to pursue Kamsarmax cover for one- to two-year employment, but bid and offer stayed apart and owners of modern eco tonnage were reluctant to chase the market lower. On balance we would characterise the tone as soft but stabilising into month-end, with near-term direction hinging on whether the Pacific's tentative firming can broaden and Atlantic cargo replenishment comes through.

This week on Capesize, we have seen a slow retreat across major Atlantic and Pacific basins. Pacific C5 West Australia/China saw relatively limited fresh cargo out of Australia with two main active miners in play. Latest last done levels on C5 reported at low-mid USD 12 levels with the most recent fixture reported at USD 12.25 for mid August dates. Refreshed ideas today are at high USD 11s and low USD 12s for mid August. C3 Brazil/China and West Africa also saw softening this week, in part due to easing oil prices earlier in the week. Charterers took a more patient approach amid the weaker market levels with bids hovering around the USD 33s for late August dates and offers aiming in the mid-low USD 34s. Ideas moving to September are rumored in the USD 32s signaling potential further softening. Atlantic activity has remained subdued this week following limited fresh interest. Transatlantic stems saw a slight increase in cargo volume but levels are below owners' expectations. Charterers are hopeful for rate corrections before committing and owners continue to discount prompt vessels in order to secure employment. Transatlantic paper has increased marginally today with C8 transatlantic valuing USD 44,500 per day.

WEST The arb has been widening all week, and freight is following; where we saw ~250 $/mt end of last week, we now see last done at high 280s $/mt and Owners last ideas between 290 and 300+. US propane stocks rose by 6.3mn/b per EIA weekly stats. Fixing activity in the West has been focused in last decade August dates, with one first decade September fixture reported. There are still a handful of ships able to meet august dates.  EAST East activity continues to be limited with some owners still waiting for any change in the Strait transits.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained subdued with limited fresh activity reported. Atlantic sentiment was mixed, with North America under pressure from longer tonnage lists, while the East Mediterranean remained relatively firmer. In Asia, conditions were mixed with softer sentiment in the North but improved activity in Southeast Asia and steady Indian Ocean demand. Handysize market remained balanced in Europe, while the US Gulf and South Atlantic continued to face pressure from tonnage availability. Overall, both markets are awaiting stronger cargo flow and increased activity for clearer direction.

The Panamax market has drifted softer through the week, with sentiment turning cautious across both basins as the index eased and owners found bids reluctant to follow their ideas. In the Atlantic the tone has been subdued – transatlantic business is holding together rather better than fronthaul, but the constraint is one of cargo volume rather than tonnage, and a build-up of ballasters arriving from the East has left forward positions in the South under pressure and the basin trading two-tier, with prompt units still commanding a premium. The Pacific has been the weaker of the two, as thin fresh grain and coal enquiry out of North Pacific, Australia and Indonesia has allowed prompt tonnage to accumulate and charterers to sit back and bid below last-done. Period remains the steadier corner of the market, with one-year business still concluding, though a backwardated forward curve and firmer bunkers on Middle East tensions are keeping owners measured rather than assertive. We look for a sideways-to-easier tone into next week, with the eventual ramp-up in new-crop grain out of the US Gulf and South America the most likely source of support later in the quarter.

This week on Cape, we saw quieter activity in the Pacific and Atlantic basins. All markets overall have fallen since last week levels with some signals of improvement. Pacific C5 sees limited miner activity and growing competition from owners. West Australia stems are limited with owners seeing low USD 11s and others claiming to see low USD 12s for first half August. Latest fixture from West Australia/Qingdao was done at USD 11.1 for August 7-9 dates. C3 Brazil/China and West Africa stems also saw slow activity this week so far, and rising bunker prices may further affect freight rates going forward. Today's offers so far are in the low-mid USD 33s for mid August dates, and ideas in the high USD 32s for end August laycans. Yesterday we heard rumors of a West Africa stem fixed in the USD 31s. North Atlantic is also quiet and we see growing tonnage lists building. The North is mostly confined to a couple transatlantic stems, and a few fresh fronthaul stems. Last night we heard of a fixture for early August in mid USD 42 levels ex Sept-Iles/Qingdao for 6-15 August on a standard Cape.

The Handy and Handymax market remained active this week, supported by a healthy mix of spot and short-period opportunities across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Cargo flow remained steady, with active tonnage circulation across key regions. Demand was primarily driven by grain, coal, fertilizer, and petcoke trades. The Atlantic basin, particularly South America, continued to generate the majority of activity, while Asia provided consistent short-haul employment opportunities.  The Supramax and Ultramax markets remained firm, although spot cargo demand has started to ease, with market attention shifting toward late July and August positions. East Coast South America (ECSA) continues to offer significantly stronger returns than West Africa, and despite the widening spread between the two regions, the U.S. Gulf market remains broadly balanced. Owners have remained selective in their voyage choices, particularly when considering repositioning opportunities as the USG continues to rise.

This week on Capes, fresh activity emerged earlier this week mostly centered around Brazil and West Africa stems with strong fixtures in the first half of the week. Today activity on C3 Brazil / China saw less activity, although players are still rating at similar levels seen earlier in the week. Latest offers on C3 Brazil/China seen for early August at mid USD 34 levels, and later dates posting offers in the high USD 32s. The Baltic exchange shows that all basins are a tick down, as well as C3, falling slightly after bunker prices saw an overnight jump.  North Atlantic trade this week has been more centered around West Africa fronthaul stems, with a fixture yesterday reported in low USD 36 levels, equivalent to USD 76.3K a day on C9.   In the Pacific, we saw a slightly suppressed tone earlier in the week, and flat market today on C5 West Australia / China, with offers in the low USD 14s and High USD 13s range for end July dates and last done levels posting low USD 13s for end July. August outlook is expected to decrease as rumours of low-mid USD 12 and low USD 13s reported.   Overall, markets look toward the bearish direction going forward across major segments, with C3 Brazil / China posting a higher daily earning potential over C5 West Australia / Qingdao.

The Panamax market held a firm but consolidating tone through the week, with the index trading broadly sideways at historically elevated levels after the sharper gains of recent weeks. In the Atlantic, fronthaul remained the engine - steady mineral and grain demand out of the US Gulf, North Coast South America and the northern basins kept owners confident on the longer east-bound legs, while East Coast South America held its ground and better-supplied transatlantic rounds left the North Atlantic waiting on fresh cargo to set the next direction. The Pacific was the steadier of the two basins, underpinned by a deep North Pacific grain book, a consistent flow of Australian and Indonesian coal, and a gradually tightening prompt list as tonnage was drawn south toward South American loading; sentiment stayed constructive and owners largely held their offers, leaving charterers to chase. Period enquiry remained active and reasonably well bid, though owners' ideas and charterers' bids stayed some way apart and the forward curve continues to sit in modest backwardation. Overall the tone is constructive-to-steady heading into next week, with firmer bunker prices and a quieter North Atlantic the principal watch-points.

WEST We have seen a lot of activity on shipping in the West during the last few weeks, and current fixing count for August now stand at 25 deals (10/10/5 by decade). Last done commercially clean deal at USD 235 HCvP on a Neo type ship, but as we still see several uncovered cargos in both 2nd and 3rd decade of August, owners latest ideas at USD 250+ HCvP.  EAST East of Suez market is again facing increased turmoil as the ceasefire between Iran and US have been broken. The relatively newly established and increasingly active STS-Sohar market may meet less willingness from owners as the market is yet again forced to reassess risk.

Sentiment in the VLGC sector improved markedly during the week, pushing USG–East TCEs above USD 100,000/day after a sharp rebound from the lows recorded last week. In the West, an active fixing pace has significantly reduced prompt tonnage availability, leaving only a handful of July positions open. As a result, freight levels have moved higher, with H/C rates climbing from the low USD 160s to around USD 210. Owners remain optimistic on the near-term outlook, supported by improving MEG demand and an increasing preference for Cape routing over Panama. At the same time, the firmer MEG outlook continues to shape decisions, with vessel positioning increasingly reflecting expectations of stronger Middle East activity and sustained support for freight levels.

As storms brew in the Pacific, strong demand continues on C5 West Australia/Brazil trade routes with offers between low-mid USD 13s. Earlier in the week we saw a series of stems for second half July dates fixing in low-mid USD 13s while other majors fixed C5 in low USD 13s and one reported selling 13 flat for end July dates. Today fresh fixtures were seen, all in low USD 13 levels. Further uncertainty awaits as Typhoon Maysak is expected to bring continued storms to already flooded regions of southern and central China, which may lead to further discharge disruptions. C3 Brazil/China trades are also at potential risk of discharge disruptions in the coming days, however markets have seen stronger offers this week, with offers in the mid USD 32s and low USD 30s for August dates. Others have seen bids in low USD 32 levels and fixtures have been reported in mid USD 32 levels for end July and early August laycans. North Atlantic activity has also picked up this week, with a recent transatlantic stem ex West Africa to Arzew fixing in the USD 10s (about USD 49.5k/day equivalent to opening Gibraltar). C8 has +5.77% gains today on paper, while C3 and C5 routes are down slightly compared to yesterday.

The Panamax market remains firm in the Atlantic, where limited prompt vessel availability, particularly in the North, continues to support owner sentiment and keep charterers under pressure for coverage. In the Pacific, it is more balanced, with quieter activity and ample tonnage offset by more cargos from the NOPAC. Indonesian demand remains soft, while potential weather disruptions around Taiwan and South China may temporarily tighten tonnages. Overall, the Atlantic is providing the main support to the market, while the Pacific remains broadly stable but regionally mixed.

On Supramax, US Gulf remains firm- demand is healthy and tonnage tight. ECSA holds steady with firmer levels for index dates, while West Africa has strengthened on a thin tonnage list plus ongoing weather delays along the coast. The Continent stays lacklustre on limited scrap volumes, and the Mediterranean, though quieter, shows signs of firming as tonnage thins. Asia remains subdued overall on weak mineral demand from Australia and Southeast Asia and limited NOPAC grains, though backhauls and renewed Indonesia x India demand are propping the region up. Handy sentiment is softer and positional across the board, with wide bid-offer spreads in the Atlantic pushing owners to reassess expectations lower, while Asia sees tonnage lengthening and rates flat. Overall tone: Atlantic cautiously positive in pockets, Asia waiting on fresh impetus.

Several deals have been concluded ex US this week from end July into 1H August, bringing total July fixtures to 23 deals and 8 for August. Freight sentiment has strengthen considerably within the last 24 hours, from last concluded fixture yesterday at around $170 HCvP, to high 180s - low 190s being reported today. In the East, there have been talks of ships subfixed to load ex MEG for July, but no deals appear to have finally been done.

The Supramax/Handysize market remained mixed, with the Atlantic showing signs of improvement while Asia continued to soften. Sentiment in the US Gulf and South Atlantic strengthened, reported better enquiry and improving momentum, particularly for transatlantic business, while the Mediterranean also saw a increase in activity, providing support to the basin. In contrast, the Pacific market remained under pressure as a lack of fresh cargo demand, particularly from South Asia, led to increasing prompt tonnage.

The Panamax market remained firm, supported by improving demand in both the Atlantic and Pacific. In the Atlantic, prompt tonnage remains relatively tight despite the emergence of more early July vessels, with strong transatlantic, mineral fronthaul and East Coast South America demand continuing to support sentiment. Owners are maintaining a firm stance, although an increase in ballasting vessels into ECSA may gradually improve tonnage availability. In the Pacific, stronger demand from Australia and the NOPAC, combined with fewer owners committing to longer trips, has tightened effective vessel supply and kept market sentiment positive.

All segments up today on Cape after a flat start to the week, C5 rates recovered as all major miners returned to market with healthy cargo volumes. High USD 10s have been most recent fixtures, with highest so far today done at USD 10.85 for a West Australia/China stem for 15-17 July, and USD 10.75 for 16-18 July dates ex Hedland/Japan. C3 Brazil/China rates have climbed over the last 3 days, with activity sharply picking up yesterday, setting a positive sentiment and more constructive tone. Latest offers on C3 have seen around USD 33 levels for 11-20 July dates, and last done was a standard Cape in the USD 31s for end July ex Brazil. Earlier week fixtures were in the mid/high USD 28-29.4 levels ex Brazil/China. Transatlantic activity picked up as of yesterday following one operator fixing a fronthaul from Sept-IIes to Taiwan for early August dates at USD 36 which is equivalent to around USD 66.7 C9 basis. Transatlantic demand continues across late July and early August dates and healthy tonnage sits tighter in end July dates. C3 21-31 July last done USD 31. C5 15-17 July last done USD 10.3, 17-19 July last done USD 10.75, 19-21 July last done USD 10.35.

Subdued activity in the VLGC market so far this week. The vessel balance in USG/USEC remains largely unchanged, however, a narrowing arbitrage has halted any new activity. In the East, we have started to see more enquires ex MEG appear following a handful of deals fixed STS Sohar week prior, but so far nothing reported fixed.

The Panamax market has remained uneven this week, with the Atlantic showing more life as fresh inquiry improved across both fronthaul and transatlantic trades. However, direction remains divided and the tonnage list looks less tight than last week. Owners are still managing to hold firmer ideas in certain pockets where prompt tonnage is tighter, but the wider basin feels broadly balanced rather than outright firm. The Pacific remains under pressure, with supply still outweighing demand despite better activity and some fresh cargo appearing, while owners are showing more resistance, particularly on longer-duration business and better-spec units. Overall sentiment remains soft, with the market continuing to ease, though the pace of decline appears to be slowing.

On Supramax, market lost some momentum after recent gains, with sentiment becoming more cautious across both basins. In the Atlantic, owners largely maintained a firm stance, although activity slowed and the market appeared increasingly positional. Elsewhere, the region seemed to be taking a natural breather following a stronger run, while arbitrage opportunities became less prominent. In Asia, limited fresh enquiry and wider bid-offer gaps weighed on sentiment, resulting in a quieter and more subdued environment. Overall, the sector remains supported by underlying optimism in the Atlantic, but short-term direction appears less clear as owners and charterers alike adopt a wait-and-see approach.   The Handy market continued to display a steady-to-firm tone overall. Atlantic regions, particularly the South Atlantic and US Gulf, remained supported by healthy demand and positive sentiment, helping maintain a constructive outlook. The Continent and Mediterranean saw more limited activity, with conditions broadly unchanged. In Asia, a balanced supply-demand picture and consistent cargo flow helped keep the market stable, with charterers generally maintaining a positive approach. Overall, the sector remains on a solid footing, supported by steady fundamentals and resilient sentiment across most regions.

This week on Capesize we have seen flat levels across the pacific earlier in the week with marginal decline today on C5. Physical fixtures for C5 West Australia/China have seen last done levels in the USD 11.25 range for early July dates and USD 11.75 for mid July. Earlier week fixtures were hovering between mid USD 11s-11.75 range for July dates. On C3 Brazil/China, a more active on fronthauls from Brazil, with active fixing yesterday. Latest fixtures today indicate levels hovering in the USD 31s with the latest stem fixed for late July dates. Earlier week fixtures were seen between mid USD 31s-33s, however Baltic today is down again slightly. In the North, tonnage demand has remained healthy with support through July dates, though transatlantic levels remained flat over the last week. West Africa cargoes have been an attractive substitute for limited fronthauls in the north. Recent fixtures ex West Africa are shown in mid USD 31 levels, with last being fixed at USD 31.5 from West Africa to China. Daily earning spreads for C3 vs C5 show stronger earning potential on C3 Brazil/China, with the latest spread around USD 8671 per day.

Over the past week, sentiment in the Supramax and Handysize sectors remained broadly positive, led by continued strength across the Atlantic basin. The US Gulf and South Atlantic markets consistently provided support, with improving confidence and healthy cargo demand underpinning activity despite limited reported fixtures. Mediterranean conditions also firmed gradually, benefiting from steady enquiry and better cargo coverage. In contrast, Asian markets were generally more balanced, with sentiment ranging from stable to mildly positive. While demand remained present, particularly for regional and long-haul employment, momentum appeared less pronounced than in the Atlantic. Overall, owners retained a positive outlook, supported by tightening vessel availability in Atlantic regions and a steady flow of cargo requirements across both vessel segments. Period appetite remains however very few fixtures reported past week.

The Panamax market presents a mixed picture, with the Atlantic outperforming the Pacific. In the Atlantic, activity has improved with better cargo replenishment, steady transatlantic and fronthaul demand, and tighter prompt tonnage supporting sentiment and helping rates remain stable. Meanwhile, the Pacific remains under pressure due to limited grain and mineral demand, an oversupply of prompt vessels, and a lack of fresh cargoes. Overall, Atlantic strength is providing some support to the broader market, but Pacific weakness continues to weigh on sentiment.

Subdued activity in the VLGC market this week as the world anxiously awaits further developments around the Straight of Hormuz. The vessel balance in USG/USEC remains largely unchanged, however, a narrowing arbitrage is halting new activity unless freight drops significantly from last done levels of mid USD 260’s basis HCvP. On the back of the shear volatility in the product market seen in the recent month or so and the arbitrage movements parallel to a potentially opening of the Straight of Hormuz, it is hard to be adamant of short term freight movements should an opening delay further.

This week on Cape we saw a decline with Pacific C5 markets remaining flat over the last days. Bids were initially reported in the low USD 10s but thanks to good support from miners, levels recently have raised to USD 10.6-10.7 levels in Pacific and last done for early July at USD 10.85. Atlantic sentiment has weakened with C3 declining sharply over the last week. Bids reported in the USD 30s with offers hovering around USD 34 for mid July dates, capping activity in the Atlantic. North Atlantic also sees softer sentiment. Recently a Newcastlemax fixed close to USD 35 on a C3 Brazil/China fixture. Baltic today is at USD 31.75 which is still marginally over the average so far this year, yet decreased 2.63% today. C5 today was flat with Baltic printing USD 10.73, slightly below the year to date average. The latest spread for Atlantic vs Pacific is USD 11400 in favour of C3 Brazil/China. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June seen offers USD 37.25, 1-10 June seen offers USD 36.75, 11-20 July last done USD 35 Newcastlemax. C5 West Australia/China 1-3 July last done USD 10.85, 4-6 July last done USD 10.5, 7-9 July last done USD 11.1.

WEST Spot fixing activity has been subdued in the West this week, except from one Asian major fixing a ship at around USD 250 HCvP for 3rd decade July via tender. Forward fixing out of the US Gulf remains limited, with just 8 spot fixtures recorded so far for July loading (3/4/1 by decade). This is a marked slowdown compared to previous months and highlights the current lack of visible cargo flow. Meanwhile, prompt ship availability remains tight, with only two VLGCs available for loading up to 10th July, and just a handful of ships for 10-15 July window. This constrained availability suggests that the market retains upside potential and could quickly firm once more cargoes emerge.  EAST MEG exports remain constrained amid the ongoing Iran situation, limiting conventional cargo flow. However, alternative setups have recently created some business, with STS cargoes reported off Sohar at premium rates. These have been fixed around USD 215 RT/CH.

The Panamax market remains divided between a gradually improving Atlantic and a weakening Pacific. Atlantic sentiment has turned slightly more constructive, supported by better transatlantic activity, firmer fronthaul demand, and increasing NCSA enquiry, although ample tonnage and wide bid-offer spreads continue to cap gains. In the Pacific, limited cargo volumes, a growing tonnage list, and cautious charterers are keeping pressure on rates, particularly on Indonesian business. While vessel tightness indicators still point to near-term softness, strong shipment volumes, supportive demand fundamentals, and a coal forward curve now moving into slight backwardation suggest the market could find better support as July approaches.

The Supramax market maintained a positive tone, supported by stronger enquiry in the Atlantic and improving activity across Asia. Market reported firmer sentiment in the US Gulf and South Atlantic, while growing backhaul demand in North Asia helped support overall vessel demand. The Handysize also strengthened, with tighter tonnage availability and balanced supply-demand conditions contributing to a firmer market environment. Activity remained steady across most regions, with the US Gulf and Asian markets showing the most encouraging signs of improvement.

A softer week on Cape with Pacific basins down from recent highs over the last week with further downward pressure expected. June C5 West Australia/China fresh fixtures indicate last done levels in the low USD 12 range with late June last done seen USD 12 flat and end June seeing USD 12.35. For Atlantic, both C3 Brazil/China and North Atlantic are trading firm with mixed sentiment. C3 Brazil/China stems see offers for late June dates in the low USD 37 range and early July offers at mid USD 36 levels. One fixture reported today was 11-20 laycan fixing USD 35 on a Newcastlemax. With strong demand and limited fresh tonnage in the North Atlantic, transatlantic routes remain firm as owners hold out for premium fronthaul rates to return amid continued tightness in the basin. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June offers USD 37.25, 1-10 July bids USD 34, offers USD 36.5, 11-20 June last done (Newcastlemax) USD 35. C5 West Australia/China 19-21 June last done USD 12, 25-27 June last done 12.35.

USG market remains quiet with limited visible fixing. Two deals reported at USD 270, with broader Apr/May activity at 48 liftings ex-Houston. Forward July coverage is still thin at just four fixtures, split between USD 270 and USD 285, pointing to a firmer tone. Most activity this week has been done discreetly, masking underlying positioning. An Asian oil major tender is currently in play and could set the next benchmark. Baltic sentiment remains stable-to-firm, supporting the view of gradual upside.

The Panamax market opened the week on a softer note, with Posidonia and regional holidays keeping activity limited and many players still reassessing direction. The Atlantic remains under pressure, with limited fresh mineral and grain enquiry meeting a growing prompt tonnage list in the Continent and Mediterranean, forcing earlier-position owners to trim expectations. ECSA is broadly flat but feels toppy for index dates, with spot tonnage still discounted due to limited cargo volume. In the Pacific, Indonesia and Australian mineral flows continue to provide some support, but sentiment has turned more cautious as tonnage builds and fresh requirements remain thin. Overall, near-term indicators still point bearish, while coal demand and potential Chinese weather disruptions remain the main upside risk.

Despite Posidonia & regional holidays around, market continued to exhibit a generally constructive tone. In the Atlantic, sentiment remained positive, particularly in USG where tightening vessel avails continued to support owners’ expectations. ECSA maintained firm underlying fundamentals, although fresh business remained limited. In Asia, it was a mixed picture, with stronger demand evident in the north while ample prompt tonnage weighed on sentiment further south. The Handy sector showed comparatively firmer momentum across Asia, supported by tightening vessel supply and steady cargo demand, helping offset the subdued activity seen across much of the Atlantic basin. With the upcoming monsoon season in India, demand is expected to slowdown in the coming weeks. Period activity remains limited with very few fixtures reported in the region.

This week on Capesize, C3 Brazil/China remains firm but thin fresh activity, with ideas hovering around USD 38 today for July stems. With slightly softening forward curve and lack of prompt tonnage we expect to see slight easing for Q3 stems. The Atlantic remains hot for another week, with transatlantic C8 pushing USD 58,000 per day and C9 at USD 76,972 reflecting strong front haul demand and limited prompt tonnage in continent. Ballasters are still favouring Brazil/China C3 but North Atlantic continue to command premium rates. C5 Pacific still remains firm but slightly off the recent highs. Some forward softness is expected coming into late June. Owners ideas are currently hovering around USD 16 and bids reported in the mid USD 15s for June 18-22 stems. C3 Brazil/China last done USD 38 21-30 June. C5 West Australia/China last done USD 15.85 16-18 June, last done USD 15.7 22-24 June.

A relatively quiet week in the VLGC market, despite the underlying tightness in vessel availability for the US Gulf. Freight levels remain at, or near, record highs. Activity has been notably subdued across regions, largely influenced by Monday’s holiday in Europe and yesterday’s holidays in both Singapore and the Middle East, resulting in limited fresh enquiry.

The Panamax/Kamsarmax market opened the week cautiously after the holidays, with sentiment still lacking conviction despite some firmer undertones. The Atlantic appears broadly balanced, with prompt tonnage largely absorbed, slimmer lists in the Continent/West Mediterranean and ECSA supported by firmer paper, while the Pacific looks more constructive on stronger Australian minerals and steady Indonesia/China demand, with owners showing more resistance. That said, the broader indicators remain bearish near-term: shipment volumes are only modestly ahead of fleet growth, coal contango has widened, and both Pacific and South Atlantic tightness indicators point to potential softening, suggesting any upside may remain fragile unless fresh cargo volumes build quickly.

This week on Capesize we saw firming across all major segments, with strong Pacific activity driving sentiment higher throughout the week. Pacific C5 markets remain firm and well supported, with activity yesterday fixing in the USD 16.10-16.5 range for early and mid June stems ex West Australia/Qingdao. With a stable to slightly bullish market, owners are holding ideas around last done levels for Pacific stems. Atlantic markets remain firm but slightly cautious, with C3 today bidding in the high USD 37s and last done at USD 38 for late June dates. Sentiment is firm yet somewhat cautious with good support despite limited fresh prompt tonnage. In the North Atlantic, we saw a quiet start to the week with slow activity. Strong fronthaul demand has caused tight transatlantic tonnage as owners continue to push for premium returns on fronthaul. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June last done USD 38. C5 West Australia/China 7-9 June last done USD 16.25, 10-12 June last done USD 16.1, 13-15 June last done USD 16.25.

The market opened this week on a relatively balanced but gradually softer footing, as parts of Europe was off on Monday - with activity mainly centred around TCT and short-period employment. In the Atlantic, continued South America grain movements supported cargo demand into both regional and Atlantic destinations, although increasing vessel availability and flexible positioning kept pressure on rates. The Supra/Ultramax segment saw a steady flow of prompt June openings globally, contributing to a more competitive tonnage list and allowing charterers to apply increased pressure in negotiations. In Asia, trading activity remained focused on regional distribution within Southeast and Northeast Asia, with cargo flow steady but insufficient to significantly tighten market conditions. Period enquiry remained active across short and long durations, though a persistent gap between owners’ ideas and charterers’ bids continued to slow longer-term conversions. Overall, the Handy and Supra markets remained stable but leaned slightly in charterers’ favour, as balanced cargo flow, ample tonnage supply and cautious fixing activity kept rates largely range-bound across most regions.

After a fairly quiet end to last week in the Pacific, Capesize demand rebounded on Monday as Port Hedland and Dampier basins firmed for June stems, with last done at USD 15 for 7-8 June dates. Pacific C5 markets are currently firm but steady with multiple trades reported in the mid USD 15 range. Tighter tonnage coming into June appears to keep levels near current highs, setting a balanced market tone for Pacific, though forward curves suggest possible easing beyond mid-June laycans. In the Atlantic, we saw exceptionally strong demand for transatlantic trade in the early week. Levels have subsided today and are active and well supported with C8 at USD 46,875/day (-10.69% compared to yesterday) and fronthaul C9 at USD 73,639 thanks to tight tonnage in the north and strong mineral demand. Ballasters continue to favour Brazil stems over transatlantic, further constraining supply. C3 Brazil/China is stable but thin today on fresh fixtures, with ideas hovering in the mid USD 36s. C3 Brazil/China 1-10 June bid USD 37 offer USD 37, 11-20 June last done 33.8, 21-30 June offer USD 36.75, 1-10 July bid USD 36 offer USD 36. C5 West Australia/China 1-3 June last done USD 15.35, 3-5 June last done USD 15.5, 4-6 June last done USD 15.

Panamax sentiment has turned softer, with the recent rally now looking increasingly tired. The Atlantic is losing support as fronthaul activity and ECSA enquiry slow, while a fuller tonnage list in the Continent and Mediterranean is adding pressure on owners’ ideas. In the Pacific, the tone is also more defensive, with limited fresh cargo, weaker paper, and prompt tonnage beginning to build, particularly in the North. Owners are still trying to hold close to last-done levels, especially for better-positioned modern units, but charterers are cautious and bids are drifting lower. Overall, the market looks close to a near-term peak, and without a fresh injection of cargo in either basin, further downside feels likely.

The spot VLGC market activity is hampered by scarce vessel availability for June laycans ex USG. As a result, the few fixtures that have been concluded during the last week have seen levels yet again setting new all time high records on a per ton basis. As of today, around twenty fixtures have been concluded for June ex USG and USEC whereas April and May saw a total of about thirty more deals done for freight. The way things are looking at the moment, it seems this situation will continue well into July and thus keep the market on a tight leash.

The market opened this week on a mixed and increasingly positional footing. In the Atlantic, sentiment remained divided view underlying demand increasing in US Gulf, although widening bid/offer spread kept activity selective. The South Atlantic softened amid easing demand and growing tonnage, while Asia saw slower momentum overall with prompt vessels in the south weighing on sentiment despite pockets of enquiry further north. Overall, both Supra and Handy market lacked clear direction as cautious trading and regional imbalances continued to dominate market sentiment.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained generally firm, with sentiment supported mainly by steady activity in Asia where balanced tonnage and cargo demand continued. The Atlantic market remained largely positional, particularly in the Continent and Mediterranean where fresh enquiry was still limited and tonnage availability remained ample. The South Atlantic showed signs of gradual improvement, while the US Gulf stayed relatively stable, although some softer sentiment was in the Supramax.

The Panamax market has continued its firm trajectory through the week, with momentum building across both basins. In the Atlantic, fronthaul remains the engine – strong NCSA grain demand is keeping cargo volumes healthy and owners confident, with the strength on longer east-bound legs allowing them to hold firm on shorter Atlantic business as well. The Pacific has moved in tandem, driven by tight prompt tonnage, improving NoPac grain stems and a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal; charterers are having to chase. Period interest is active but bid and offer remain apart. The overall tone is constructive heading into next week.

Freight rates continue to surge to fresh highs despite an increasingly challenging arbitrage backdrop, underscoring that control has firmly shifted in favour of shipping. June spot activity remains exceptionally limited, with the current fixture count at just 18 liftings (8/7/3 by decade), a stark contrast to the high‑40s average observed over the past two months. Although some incremental volumes may still materialize as voyage itineraries firm up, the availability of June U.S. positions remains critically constrained. This persistent tightness is expected to sustain upward pressure on freight levels in the near term.

This week on Capesize, we see firmer markets overall today with increases in every route. June demand on C3 Brazil/China remains firm while C5 West Australia/China takes a more balanced tone as C5 improves today after being relatively flat early week (however levels have jumped 4.7% on paper today). Pacific C5 West Australia/China sees more activity today with multiple stems fixed between USD 15.15-15.30s from West Australia to Qingdao. Despite a softening FAA curve moving forward, spot sentiment remains bullish on tight tonnage and if momentum holds, late May laycans are expected to climb around USD 16s levels. On C3 Brazil/China remains the stronger leg with firm demand coming into June with multiple fixtures done in the USD 36.25-37 range for mid-June laycans. West Africa stems are slightly lower at mid USD 35 levels. Atlantic sees stronger transatlantic activity over the last few days, supporting overall market levels and promoting strong demand for prompt tonnage. Sentiment remains bullish for short term transatlantic and fronthaul positions out from Atlantic. C3 1-10 June: bids at USD 37, 11-20 June: last done USD 33.8. C5 13-15 May: last done USD 15.8, 25-27 May: last done USD 16.6, 28-30 May: last done USD 15.15.

VLGC freight market remains tight with Owners latest ideas pushing into $300s HCvP for US business. We count 14 spot fixtures in June thus far (8/5/1 by decade), compared to 48 deals seen in May and 47 in April. We currently see less than a handful of ships that can be worked firm today for June, and it remains to be seen where the next deals will be fixed at.

Supramax market started the week quieter, with sentiment generally steady but lacking fresh momentum. The Atlantic showed some positivity, particularly for fronthaul demand from USG, while other areas remained slow. Handy followed a similarly subdued tone overall, though the Atlantic saw pockets of improved demand, especially in the USG and South Atlantic. In contrast, the Continent and Mediterranean continued to soften with limited fresh cargo. Asia remained relatively stable, supported by tighter tonnage and steady demand despite the slow start. Looking back to the prior session, both segments were already losing steam ahead of the holidays, with weak activity in the Atlantic and limited cargo flow in Asia. Overall, the market remains cautious, with sentiment varying by region.

This week on Capesize, we see strengthening across every segment, with C3 and C5 remaining well supported near future. C5 leads the charge as of yesterday as the highest time charter earner, today gaining an additional 6.5% on paper. Recent fixtures for C5 West Australia/China have been reported in the mid-high USD 14 for second half May stems and early June bids are coming in the mid USD 15s with offers in the range of USD 15.75-16. Overall, the Pacific market is outperforming index with firm bids and rising offers looking positive with potential for future gains coming into June. For C3 Brazil/China, market remains firm but slightly capped with fresh offers in the mid USD 37s for early June stems. West Africa stems are still in circulation with no distinct premiums over Brazil stems. North Atlantic transatlantic remains firmly bid, supported by strong mineral demand and limited prompt tonnage. Sentiment remains positive as the North Atlantic continues to outperform paper, underpinned by healthy Coal and Iron Ore flow. C3 11-20 May offer USD 30.75, 1-10 June offer USD 36, 11-20 June offer USD 37.25. C5 19-21 May bid USD 15.3 / offer USD 15.85 / last done USD 15.9.

This week the Panamax market has turned firmer after a quieter start, with sentiment improving across both basins. In the Atlantic, early pressure from a longer Continent tonnage list and limited transatlantic demand has eased as NCSA grain activity picked up, giving owners more confidence and pushing fronthaul levels higher, while ECSA remains supported by steady demand and tighter prompt tonnage. USG activity is still relatively flat and transatlantic volumes remain thin, but the tone is clearly more constructive. In the Pacific, the market remains firm despite some Golden Week disruption, with Australia and Indonesia coal/mineral demand providing the main support, prompt tonnage looking tight, and modern/premium units in particularly short supply. With China back in the market and Japan returning, activity is picking up and owners are again showing stronger resistance.

The period market remained active this week, with demand centred on short to medium-term employment. Charterers continued to prioritize flexibility, while longer-term discussions remained selective and focused mainly on modern, fuel-efficient tonnage. Interest was strongest for versatile vessels offering flexible trading, grain-clean holds, GOA transit, and suitability for steel and project cargoes. Tonnage availability remained ample across both Atlantic and Pacific basins, with a steady flow of prompt and forward positions, including modern eco vessels and newbuildings. Owners remained disciplined, particularly for quality employment, maintaining a noticeable bid-offer gap as charterers continued to test lower levels, especially for one-year business. Modern, efficient vessels continued to command the strongest interest, while older or less flexible units faced increased competition. Overall, market conditions remain constructive, with steady enquiry and healthy fixing activity, although longer-term commitments continue to be approached cautiously.

We have registered 7-8 fixtures this week for June. The market continues to tighten, underpinned by a scarcity of available vessels from end May/early June onwards. Based on current BLPG 3 levels, modern conventionally fueled VLGCs are now generating round‑trip earnings of approximately USD 130,000 per day, marking the strongest market returns since the latter part of 2023. Owners and trader relets are increasingly testing higher ideas, with ideas shown up to USD 260 per tonne HC on Pmax ship. Given the absence of meaningful tonnage availability through at least 10 June, downside risk to freight remains limited. The return of a more standard five‑week fixing window next week should help sustain momentum and drive further fixtures. In contrast, the MEG market remains quiet, with uncertainty persisting around the Straits of Hormuz and the timing and scale of any cargo flow resumption.

This week on Capesize, C3 Brazil/China market remains firm but tense. Owners are resilient, holding offers in the USD 33-33.75 range for second half May, with last done at USD 31.9 for 21-31 May. The C3 FFA is reported to soften after May, adding pressure on later positions. Currently C3 is the stronger market compared to C5 with a dollar per day differential of USD +914 on C3. The C5 market also remains active and bullish with current spreads at sub USD 13 bids vs USD 13.1-13.3 offers. Multiple stems were cleared yesterday, and cargo lists from West Australia remain healthy. C5 is leading sentiment with solid grain stems and strong demand, while C3 market remains rangebound but supported. North Atlantic market is strong this week with fronthaul C9 stems commanding USD 67,000/day. FAA May is at USD 16.35 for C7 Bolivar/Rotterdam while Baltic sets C7 at USD 18.96 reflecting tight tonnage in the basin. With tight tonnage in the North and limited fresh fixtures reported, bullish sentiment remains amongst owners. C3 11-20 May: offer USD 33.25, 21-31 May: last done USD 31.9, 1-10 June: offer USD 33.5, 11-20 June: bid USD 32.5, offer USD 33.5. C5 14-16 May: bid USD 12.9, offer USD 13, last done USD 13.5, 17-19 May: bid USD 12.85, offer USD 13.35, last done USD 13.1.

The Panamax market opened the week with a clear Atlantic/Pacific split. The Atlantic remains under pressure, with more tonnage appearing in the North Continent and limited fresh TA demand, leaving both round and fronthaul levels exposed. USG/NCSA enquiry has been patchy, while ECSA remains the one firmer pocket for forward dates, though prompt ships still face pressure to discount or wait. In the Pacific, sentiment remains more positive, supported by steady Indo/Australian coal and mineral demand ahead of Golden Week, with charterers gradually moving closer to owners’ ideas. Overall, the Atlantic feels cargo-short, while the Pacific remains better balanced and firming.

Activity in the VLGC market has indeed quiet down, however, end May chartering appetite still persists. Similar to last week, the vessel availability in the market for end of May and early June laycans ex USG is outnumbered by uncovered freight requirements. An Indonesian oil major freight tender was concluded for very end May today. The Baltic LPG 3 print is currently hovering USD 230 per ton and does not seem to budge. There are a handful of cargoes reportedly being discussed, either for chartering or FOB sales and we expect the market to continue sideways to slightly upwards from the USD 225-230 per ton mark.

Market opened the week cautious, but sentiment improved into Tuesday with momentum building across sizes. Atlantic remained somewhat mixed with USG showing signs of plateauing while South Atlantic stayed finely balanced; Continent-Mediterranean continued to lack fresh push. Asia was the main support, holding steady earlier before firming on tighter tonnage and improved northern enquiry. Supramax space saw better activity into midweek, particularly on Pacific rounds, while Indonesia runs remained well supported. Handys sector extended gains through the week, with owners gradually regaining leverage amid tighter supply. Atlantic Handy markets stayed constructive overall, though largely positional without strong fresh catalysts. Asian Handy segment continued its upward trend, driven by prompt tightness and healthier cargo flow. Overall tone improving, but still some caution lingering with players watching macro direction closely.

Panamax has started the week on a quieter footing with limited fixing reported, but the market still feels generally well supported. In the Atlantic, fronthaul and transatlantic enquiry remains in the background, with grains and NCSA continuing to lend support, although a wider bid/offer spread is keeping a lid on volume. In the Pacific, Indonesia remains the key driver, where tighter prompt tonnage and requirement-specific business is keeping owners firm, while Australia and NoPac are a touch more selective. Overall, while a small correction cannot be ruled out after the recent push, the underlying tightness on both sides suggests any dip should be limited for now.

This week on Cape we see C3 having strong premiums over C5, compared to last week’s more favorable spreads for C5. C3 is current fixing at strong mid USD 30s with fresh bids for end-May seen at USD 32.25-32.75 for C3 Brazil/China, while West Africa/China options hover around USD 34.75-35. C5 this week has been range-bound around USD 13.40-13.60 as charterers add pressure to trim levels. With tight tonnage coming into early May, miners are holding firm and sentiment remains bullish in the short term. Pacific market tone is firm but volatile. Atlantic market remains firm as North Atlantic tonnage remains tight in the basin. Ballasters from Continent are still favoring transatlantic round voyages, but strong fronthaul demand keeps sentiment positive. April 22nd differential C3 TCE USD 35,796 vs C5 TCE USD 34,353. C3 Brazil/China 21-31 May: bids USD 32.75, offers USD 34.75, 11-20 June: bids USD 32.75, offers USD 34.75. C5 22-24 Apr: bids USD 12.9, offers USD 13.35 with last done at USD 13.2-13.60, 6-8 May: bids USD 12.9, offers USD 13.35 with last done at USD 13.2.

Spot activity out of the USG accelerated further last week, with more than 25 fixtures reported. Rates have surged from around USD 170/t a week ago to as high as USD 225/t H/C via Panama Canal - the strongest level seen in over two years. At USD 225/t, earnings equate to approximately USD 115,000/day TCE for a modern conventionally fuelled VLGC, while current ask for freight is at $250/t, but we have not heard reports of any deals concluded at these record high levels yet. The recent intense fixing activity, combined with ongoing Panama Canal congestion forcing ships to sail via Cape of Good Hope, has effectively absorbed most available tonnage ex‑USG through early June. This tightening of supply is particularly notable given the absence of AG exports for the past six weeks.

This week on Capesize, we saw strengthening across all major segments. Both basins are active and trading above paper, with C3 in USD 32 and C5 pushing mid USD 13s. Charterers continue to look for Brazil and West Africa options but fixing remains slow for the time being while second half May ballaster lists build. In the North Atlantic we see limited fresh transatlantic demand. Sentiment remains steady to firm. Pacific C5 market firms further today with upward momentum and active early trading. Current range is USD 13-13.5 with last done at USD 13.3 for late April dates. Overall pacific tonnage is tight in West Australia for late April and early May dates, setting a strong bullish bias. Overall both basins C3 (Brazil/China) and C5 (West Australia/China) remain active with cautiously bullish short term sentiment. C3 (Brazil/China) 1-10 May bids USD 29.75, offers USD 33, 11-20 May bids USD 31, offers USD 32, 21-31 May bids USD 30.75. C5 (West Australia/China) 25-27 April last done USD 13.3, 28-30 April last done at USD 13.3.

The Supramax and Handysize markets maintained a generally positive tone. The Supra market, sentiment stayed firm despite a slow start to the week and a continued standoff between owners and charterers. The US Gulf and South Atlantic showed some strength, while the Continent and Mediterranean remained subdued. The Pacific provided the main support, with steady cargo flow and tighter tonnage helping sustain momentum. The Handysize market followed a similar but more subdued pattern, with limited activity overall. The Atlantic appeared mostly balanced, with some firmness in the South Atlantic, while the Pacific remained the key supportive region.

The Panamax market has carried a firmer tone this week across both basins, with owners generally holding their ground and showing little urgency, particularly in the Atlantic where fronthaul continues to lead the way on the back of steady mineral and grain demand. The North has been a touch mixed with some visible tonnage still around, but overall sentiment remains constructive as charterers are finding it difficult to pull ideas back, while ECSA has shown better enquiry and feels tighter than it did at the start of the week. In the Pacific, momentum has clearly improved, with healthy cargo flow out of Australia and Indonesia, tightening prompt tonnage and a more confident owner mindset, leaving the basin feeling progressively better as the week has developed.

LPG activity remains robust in the USG. Freight levels are firming with levels now pushing into the USD 180+ range. So far in May, approximately 34 fixtures have been concluded ex‑USG, compared to a total of 47 spot fixtures completed in April. Market sentiment remains constructive, underpinned by limited prompt availability and sustained chartering interest. Further upside potential remains should a ceasefire materialise in the AG, which could tighten tonnage further and support additional rate strength - though visibility on timing and impact remains limited at this stage. Overall, the market continues to display a firm tone, with Owners maintaining leverage as Charterers compete for available cover.

Panamax has been a bit mixed this week, but overall the tone feels steady to slightly firmer. Fronthaul business has continued to do most of the work, especially with decent grain demand ex USG, NCSA and a still solid ECSA market where April remains tight, while May is a little slower to build. In the Pacific, things have gradually improved as the week has gone on, helped by firmer FFAs, a shorter tonnage list and better cargo flow, with NoPac and Australia giving the basin most of its support. Transatlantic, though, is still the weaker part of the market and is keeping a lid on things a bit, so while owners are generally holding their ground, it still feels like we need a bit more conviction from charterers before the market can properly push on.

A modest number of fresh orders emerged mid-week; however, overall activity remained limited across both the Handysize and Supramax segments, as market participants continue to monitor ongoing geopolitical developments. The conflict in the MEG has effectively removed a portion of trading activity, with shipowners showing reluctance to conclude fixtures in the region due to heightened risk. The Handysize market remained subdued over the Easter period. Vessel availability has continued to increase, while a lack of fresh cargo enquiries has contributed to a growing tonnage surplus, exerting downward pressure on freight levels. A similar trend is observed in the Supramax and Ultramax segments. Tonnage lists have expanded, particularly in the Atlantic basin, where limited cargo volumes have resulted in reduced fixing activity and softer market conditions. Overall, persistent geopolitical uncertainty continues to weigh on sentiment, leaving the market cautious and without a clear directional trend.

This week on Capesize, Pacific trades steady but slightly softer. C5 (West Australia/China) stems have seen multiple fixtures done at USD 12.25-12.4 for 21-24 April dates. Overall Pacific tone is firm but under pressure. In the Atlantic we are seeing firm undertones but two tiered, with steady activity for Brazil and West Africa stems. Physical offers for mid-May laycans are still seeing high USD 31-32, with some guiding 32 on standard Cape for Brazil/Qingdao C3 stems. North Atlantic tonnage remains tight, keeping owners bullish for transatlantic and fronthaul runs. Transatlantic routes are steady with selective upside on fronthaul, supported by firm Pacific returns. Overall, the Cape market has regained traction post-holiday. C3 (Brazil/China) 21-30 April offers USD 30.75, 1-10 May offers USD 31.8, 11-20 May offers USD 32. C5 (West Australia/China) 21-23 April fixtures done USD 12.25, 22-24 April fixtures done USD 12.4.

The Supramax market remained soft across both basins, with limited fresh enquiries and rates easing slightly overall. Atlantic market was mixed, with the Continent and Mediterranean under pressure from tonnage build-up, while the South Atlantic basin held a more stable tone; USG continued to trend weaker amid oversupply of tonnages. In Asia, sentiment stayed subdued with rates mostly flat to slightly lower despite steady cargo flow. Handysize saw a similarly mixed-to-soft environment, with limited activity in the Continent/Mediterranean and a softer tone in the USG due to slower demand. The South Atlantic showed some improvement with firmer undertones, while Asian markets remained largely balanced with stable fundamentals. Overall, both segments continue to face muted demand and ample tonnage, keeping sentiment cautious in the near term.

3 deals registered ex US this week, taking the total fixture count in April to 47 (13/10/24 by decade) and in May to 16 (13/3/0 by decade). Last done fixed for May loading reported at USD 164 HCvP, versus the high USD 160s/low USD 170s seen week prior. As MEG trade remains effectively closed, we are now starting to see the full effect of more ships arriving USG from May onwards. We expect market to stay quiet until next week with the upcoming Easter holidays.

This week on Capesize, Pacific C5 market remains steady but firming coming into Easter. Recent fixtures reported at low USD 11s for mid-April dates and sub USD 12 for later April for C5 (West Australia/China). Earlier this week Cyclone Narelle briefly disrupted operations in Western Australia, but volumes overall remained steady. C3 (Brazil/China) sees sentiment stable to firm, supported by FFA curve and positional tightness for May dates. Recent fixtures are in the high USD 28s ex West Africa and low USD 32s ex Brazil. Ideas are USD 31.5-32 for May dates. In the North Atlantic, transatlantic demand remains steady with tight tonnage ex Continent/Baltic. C3 (Brazil/China) 21-31 April: bids USD 28, offers USD 31.5, 1-10 May: offers USD 32, 11-20 May: ideas USD 32. C5 (West Australia/China) 13-15 April: last done USD 11.25, 19-21 April: offers at USD 11.65.

The Panamax market carried a generally softer tone this week, with the Atlantic showing some signs of stabilizing while the Pacific remained under clear pressure from an oversupplied tonnage list and limited fresh cargo demand. In the Atlantic, activity improved modestly, with firmer sentiment out of ECSA and better support for fronthaul business from the US, although transatlantic remained relatively thin and prompt tonnage, particularly in ECSA, continued to trade at discounted levels. By contrast, the Pacific stayed bearish throughout. As owners were forced to soften ideas further, charterers continued to pick off the cheaper tonnage, and the lack of any meaningful fresh enquiry kept values edging lower. Overall, the market still feels cautious and directionless heading into the Easter holiday period, with any stronger late-week push in the Atlantic still to be proven.

Continued disruption in the Middle East has brought AG trading to a complete halt, with the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, injecting a high degree of uncertainty into the market. After an initial softening in rates two weeks ago, Owners have since responded by decisively hardening their rate expectations, most notably in the USG where fixing activity has gathered pace. Thirteen fixtures have already been concluded ex‑USG for the first decade of May, with recent business reported around USD 170 pmt H/C via Panama, translating to approximately USD 75,000/day TCE on a standard vessel. Despite the potential arrival of some AG ballasters, the removal of AG liftings from the supply chain has kept tonnage constrained and arbitrage firmly open. Any incremental supply has been swiftly absorbed as Charterers rushed to secure Far East cover. The current position list shows twelve vessels open for early May, despite thirteen spot fixtures already concluded for loading in the first ten days of the month. April has proven to be a record‑breaking month, with 45 spot fixtures concluded out of the USG, including 21 fixed for last‑decade April loading-underscoring the strength of demand and the firmly Owner‑led tone of the market.

This week on Capesize, the Pacific continues to trade steady to firm with overall market tone firming slightly. C5 (West Australia/China) sees fixtures in the range of USD 11.55-11.85 for early April dates, and high USD 12s for Newcastlemaxes and COA linked stems. Tone has softened from previous day highs but West Australian positions for early April remain in demand with several prompt vessels in North China towards the end of March. In the Atlantic, Brazil/West Africa markets are firm but two tiered. Physical bids for C3 (Brazil/China) are heard around mid USD 30s for late April and early May dates, while early April dates see fixtures at USD 28.75. North Atlantic sees limited fresh activity, tight tonnage and strong FAA support, keeping a positive sentiment.
